section.title: Come and See What God Has Done
section.sectionRationale: A hymn calling all the earth to make a joyful noise to God, remembering the exodus deliverance through sea and river, this psalm moves from corporate praise of God's awesome deeds to personal testimony of a worshiper who was tested like refined silver, brought through fire and water, and heard when he cried out with an honest, sin-free heart.
section.thesis: The God who parted the sea for Israel's exodus, refines His people like silver through fire and water, and hears the prayer of an honest heart, calling every nation to come and see His deeds and every believer to come and hear what He has personally done for their soul.
section.frameNote: Three movements: a summons for all the earth to make a joyful noise and come see God's awesome deeds, verses 1-7; corporate praise for testing His people like silver and bringing them through fire and water into abundance, verses 8-12; and personal testimony of vows fulfilled, testing endured, and prayer heard because the heart was kept honest, verses 13-20.

units.label: Make a joyful noise to God
units.note: a summons for all the earth to see His awesome deeds

verses.text: Make a joyful noise to God, all the earth!
Sing the glory of His name; make His praise glorious.
Say to God, "How awesome are Your deeds! So great is Your power that Your enemies cower before You.
All the earth bows down to You; they sing praise to You; they sing praise to Your name." Selah
Come and see the works of God; how awesome are His deeds toward mankind.
He turned the sea into dry land; they passed through the waters on foot; there we rejoiced in Him.
He rules forever by His power; His eyes watch the nations. Do not let the rebellious exalt themselves. Selah

units.label: You have refined us like silver
units.note: tested and brought through fire and water into abundance

verses.text: Bless our God, O peoples; let the sound of His praise be heard.
He preserves our lives and keeps our feet from slipping.
For You, O God, have tested us; You have {{tsaraph|refined}} us like silver.
You led us into the net; You laid burdens on our backs.
You let men ride over our heads; we went through fire and water, but You brought us into abundance.

units.label: God has surely heard
units.note: personal testimony of vows fulfilled and prayer heard

verses.text: I will enter Your house with burnt offerings; I will fulfill my vows to You,
the vows that my lips promised and my mouth spoke in my distress.
I will offer You fatlings as burnt offerings, with the fragrant smoke of rams; I will offer bulls and goats. Selah
Come and listen, all you who fear God, and I will declare what He has done for me.
I cried out to Him with my mouth and praised Him with my tongue.
If I had cherished {{aven|iniquity}} in my heart, the Lord would not have listened.
But God has surely heard; He has attended to the sound of my prayer.
Blessed be God, who has not rejected my prayer or withheld from me His loving devotion!

tsaraph.gloss: To refine or smelt, applying intense heat to remove impurity from precious metal. God's testing of His people is pictured as this deliberate, purposeful refining, painful but productive, unlike random or purposeless suffering.

aven.gloss: Iniquity, wickedness, trouble, often connected to idolatry or deceit. The psalmist ties answered prayer directly to not cherishing this in the heart, teaching that an honestly kept heart, not sinless perfection, is what keeps the channel of prayer open.

basic.context: This psalm calls the whole earth to see God's awesome deeds, remembering how He turned the sea into dry land at the exodus. It then turns personal, a worshiper testifying that God tested him like refined silver, brought him through fire and water, and heard his prayer because he did not cherish sin in his heart.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm moves naturally from corporate praise of God's historical deeds to individual testimony, showing that the God who acted for the whole nation also personally tests and hears the individual believer.
basic.originalLanguages: God tsaraph, refines, His people like silver, verse 10, a deliberate, purposeful testing rather than random suffering. And the psalmist ties answered prayer to not cherishing aven, iniquity, in the heart, verse 18, an honestly kept heart rather than sinless perfection.
basic.typology: God turning the sea into dry land so His people passed through on foot, verse 6, recalls the exodus and anticipates the greater deliverance through Christ, who leads His people through death itself into resurrection life, just as Israel passed through the sea into freedom.
basic.christ: Christ is the one through whom God's people are truly brought 'through fire and water... into abundance,' verse 12, His own death and resurrection the pattern and power by which every trial of His people finally issues not in destruction but in overflowing life, Romans 8:37.
basic.god: God is shown as the sovereign ruler of every nation whose historic deeds, like parting the sea, call for universal praise, and as the personal refiner of His people, testing them like silver, yet also the one who hears and answers the honest prayer of a kept heart.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 14:21-22 records God turning the sea into dry land, the historic deed this psalm recalls. 1 Peter 1:6-7 compares trials to the refining of gold by fire, echoing this psalm's image of testing like silver. James 5:16 teaches that the prayer of a righteous person is powerful and effective, echoing this psalm's link between an honest heart and answered prayer.
basic.oneStory: The exodus deliverance through the sea and the personal testing of the psalmist through fire and water both anticipate the greater deliverance accomplished in Christ, who leads His people through every trial, even death itself, into the abundance of resurrection life.

context.literary:
Psalm 66 is built like a hinge. The first twelve verses speak in the plural, 'our God,' 'us,' 'we,' and the last eight in the singular, 'I,' 'my lips,' 'my prayer.' Verse 13 is the turning point: 'I will enter Your house with burnt offerings.' The choir falls silent and one voice steps out of it. What makes the design work is that the two halves are really one act of worship. The individual's vow is paid inside the great congregation, and the nation's story is told so that one person can find a place in it.

Three Selahs mark the joints, at verses 4, 7 and 15, and each follows a burst of praise or a warning. The first half climbs in three invitations. Verses 1 to 4 call the earth to sing. Verses 5 to 7 say 'Come and see,' and point to the sea. Verses 8 to 12 call the peoples to bless God for what He has done to 'us.' The second half answers with a matching pair of invitations, verse 13 to 15 for the vow and verse 16 'Come and listen,' so that seeing the deeds of God turns into hearing one person's account of them.

Notice also how the subject of the verbs moves. In verses 1 to 7 God acts on the world and the nations: enemies cower, the sea dries, His eyes watch. In verses 8 to 12 He acts on His own people, and the verbs turn hard: tested, led into the net, laid burdens, let men ride over our heads. Only in the last line of the section does the direction reverse, 'but You brought us into abundance.' The second half then closes the frame. It begins with burnt offerings at God's house and ends, in verse 20, with praise that God 'has not rejected my prayer or withheld from me His loving devotion.' The psalm begins with the whole earth and ends with the loving devotion shown to one worshiper.
context.historical:
The psalm names no author and no occasion, and that silence is part of its usefulness. Its two historical anchors are the sea and the trials. The sea in verse 6 is the Red Sea of Exodus 14, but the next phrase, 'they passed through the waters on foot,' also recalls the crossing of the Jordan, when the river was cut off and the people went over on dry ground, Joshua 3:14-17. The verb tenses in Hebrew are fluid enough that singers could sing 'there we rejoiced in Him' as if they were standing on the shore. At Passover and the other great feasts Israel was taught to see itself in the exodus, Deuteronomy 6:21-23, and this line lets a later congregation do so.

The trials of verses 10 to 12 are harder to place. 'Net,' 'burdens' and men riding 'over our heads' sound like defeat and subjugation, and some readers connect them with the Assyrian invasion in Hezekiah's day or with the exile. The psalm does not say, and it does not need to. What it gives is a pattern Israel knew well: siege, loss, survival, return to a place of fullness.

The second half describes sacrifice as the first hearers practised it. A worshiper who had made a vow 'in my distress,' verse 14, came to the sanctuary to fulfil it with burnt offerings, and the vow offering was shared with family and guests in a meal, Leviticus 7:16 and Psalm 116:14-18. Bulls, rams and goats, verse 15, are the gifts of someone who can afford it, which fits a person of means who has been delivered, but the larger point is that a vow was a debt of gratitude. The psalm has the vow said aloud in front of 'all you who fear God,' verse 16, because public testimony was part of the payment.
context.canonical:
The psalm sits in a pair with Psalm 67, and both are prayers of a people who want the nations to see. Psalm 66 tells the nations to come and see, and Psalm 67 asks God to bless Israel so that the nations will fear Him. Together they form a small missionary movement inside the Psalter. The invitation in Psalm 66:5, 'Come and see the works of God,' echoes Psalm 46:8, where the works include making wars cease, and stands beside Psalm 96:3 and Psalm 98:1-3.

The imagery of passing through water and fire is taken up by Isaiah 43:2, 'When you pass through the waters, I will be with you... When you walk through the fire, you will not be scorched.' There God promises what the psalm looks back on. The refining image is used of Israel in Isaiah 48:10, Zechariah 13:9 and Malachi 3:2-3, and of the church in 1 Peter 1:6-7, where faith is 'refined by fire' and proves genuine. Proverbs 17:3 gives the maxim behind it: the crucible is for silver, but the LORD tests hearts.

The prayer question in verse 18 belongs with a long line of texts about the cherished sin that blocks a hearing: Isaiah 59:1-2, Proverbs 28:9, Psalm 34:15-16 and the blind man's sharp remark in John 9:31. The last verse, with its note of praise for God's loving devotion, anticipates the New Testament's 'sacrifice of praise,' Hebrews 13:15, and Paul's call to present our bodies as living sacrifices, Romans 12:1. Revelation 15:3-4 sings the song of Moses and of the Lamb, with nations coming to worship, and it reads like the goal toward which Psalm 66 has been pointing all along.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The writer wants a congregation to do two things in the same breath. First, to say out loud that God's past deeds are theirs: 'there we rejoiced in Him,' verse 6, is a line that turns history into present membership. Second, to accept that the road to praise goes through pressure. Verses 10 to 12 are candid about what God did. The psalmist does not write 'the enemy did this' or 'fate did this'; he writes 'You have tested us... You led us into the net.' The claim is large: God governs even the bad years, and they were not wasted.

The second half teaches by example. A man who has been heard does not keep it to himself. He calls the God-fearers to 'come and listen,' verse 16, and he lets them hear the whole story, including the honesty of his own heart, verse 18. The aim is to give other sufferers the same ground to stand on, and to make the vow a public act of gratitude rather than a private settlement.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm records one community's history and one worshiper's vow. Nothing in it commands a particular sacrifice, and Christians do not bring burnt offerings to a temple. What it describes is pattern: God tests, God brings through, and the delivered person pays back in public praise. What it prescribes, by its shape, is a posture: join the congregation's memory, tell your own story aloud, keep your heart honest before you pray.

Be careful with verses 10 to 12. They describe how these people read their own trials, not a rule that every hardship has a purpose that can be read off at once. Job's friends made that mistake. The psalm speaks from the far side of the fire, 'but You brought us into abundance,' and it is meant to be sung by people who have come through, or who trust they will.

debates.question: Who is the 'I' of verses 13 to 20?

views.label: An individual worshiper
views.case: The voice moves from 'we' to 'I' with vows, burnt offerings and a personal story of answered prayer in verses 13 to 19. The language is that of a private thanksgiving, like Psalm 116, offered at the temple in the hearing of the God-fearers.

views.label: The king or a leader speaking for the nation
views.case: Some hear a representative voice, a king who leads the nation in thanksgiving after deliverance, and point to royal psalms where the king's vows and the people's victory are joined, such as Psalm 18 and Psalm 20. The large offerings of verse 15 suit that setting.

views.label: The nation speaking as one person
views.case: Israel is often addressed or described in the singular elsewhere, and the two halves are united by the same story of testing and rescue. The 'I' would then be the people, whose corporate experience in verses 8 to 12 is now told as one life.

debates.bearing: Nothing in the psalm requires one reading. On each of them the individual is joined to a community, and the psalm models how a person can speak personally without leaving the congregation's story. That is enough to use it in worship today.

debates.question: What exactly does verse 18 say about sin and prayer?

views.label: Cherished sin blocks prayer
views.case: The verb points to looking at something with favour or approval. If the psalmist had held on to iniquity in his heart, God would not have listened. Isaiah 59:2 and Proverbs 28:9 say something similar, and the verse works as a warning against double-minded prayer.

views.label: A claim of integrity in this case
views.case: The 'if' is a test the psalmist says he passed. Its direct aim is to explain why this prayer was answered, not to lay down a universal rule. Other psalms make the same appeal to a clear conscience, Psalm 7:3-5 and Psalm 26:1-6, without claiming sinlessness.

views.label: A reminder that answered prayer rests on grace
views.case: The parallel verse 20 credits God's loving devotion, not the psalmist's record. The 'if' protects against using God for selfish ends, but the answer itself is mercy, so believers who are aware of their failures can still pray with hope, Psalm 130:3-4.

debates.bearing: Read together, the verse guards against hypocrisy without making prayer a reward for perfection. The heart has to be honest, and the hearing still rests on God's chesed, as verse 20 says.

study.originalLanguages:
Four features of the Hebrew repay a closer look. First, the verb in verse 3, rendered 'cower,' is the same verb that in other places means to lie or to feign. It is used of enemies in Psalm 18:44 and Deuteronomy 33:29. The submission of God's enemies may be forced and unwilling, the kind of surrender that comes when power is overwhelming. Verse 4 then sets beside it the true worship of 'all the earth,' and the contrast is between a reluctant bow and a joyful song.

Second, the phrase in verse 9, 'keeps our feet from slipping,' uses the image of the foot that does not give way, found in Psalm 121:3 and Psalm 38:16. God does not remove the path through fire and water; He steadies the feet on it. The long description of trials in verses 10 to 12 sits in between two such assurances of preserved life, verse 9 before and verse 12b after.

Third, the word for 'abundance' in verse 12 comes from a root about being saturated, like ground drenched with rain or a person who has drunk his fill. It is the same noun that Psalm 23:5 uses when it says the cup 'overflows.' The destination of the journey through water and fire is not bare survival. It is a place where there is more than enough. That makes a striking contrast with the land of dry ground in verse 6: the people came through water onto dry land, and then through fire and water onto a land of saturation.

Fourth, the vow in verses 13 and 14 'that my lips promised and my mouth spoke in my distress' uses a verb that means to open wide or to part, as lips do when someone speaks without holding back. Vows made in a crisis were serious, and Ecclesiastes 5:4-5 warns against making them lightly and forgetting them. The psalm shows a man who did not forget. Finally, verse 20 closes with chesed, 'loving devotion,' the covenant word for God's steadfast faithfulness, and that one word explains everything before it. The testing, the net and the deliverance are all held inside the faithfulness of a God who keeps His promises.

Two smaller notes. The Hebrew of verse 17 can be read either 'I cried out to Him with my mouth' or, as the BSB footnote suggests, 'His praise was on my tongue,' so the psalmist is either describing the order of events, cry then praise, or saying that praise was already in his mouth as he prayed. Both fit the same heart. And the word 'Selah' at verses 4, 7 and 15 is a musical or liturgical marker whose exact meaning is unknown, but each one here comes just after a line that invites a pause: the earth bowing, God's watching eyes, the smoke of rams.

typology.type: The sea turned into dry land, verse 6
typology.fulfillment: Israel crossed the water on foot and found on the far side a people freed from slavery, Exodus 14:21-22 and 15:1-2. Paul says the whole nation was 'baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea,' 1 Corinthians 10:1-2. The correspondence is that a people are brought through water to a new life. In Christ the escalation is that He goes through death itself, Hebrews 2:14-15, and the baptised pass with Him into new life, Romans 6:3-4. The type falls short in one way: Israel's crossing did not remove sin or death from those who crossed, and most of that generation fell in the wilderness, 1 Corinthians 10:5.

The crucible gives the image of trials that burn away what is false and leave what is pure. Peter takes this up when he says that the genuineness of faith, 'more precious than gold,' is tested by fire, 1 Peter 1:6-7. The pattern is fulfilled in Christ, who 'learned obedience from what He suffered,' Hebrews 5:8, and was 'made perfect through suffering,' Hebrews 2:10. The escalation is that Christ was not refined from any impurity, because He had none, but shared the furnace for our sake. The type falls short in that a believer's refining does remove dross, while Christ's suffering was the ground of a purity that was never in doubt.

typology.type: The vow paid in God's house, verses 13 to 15
typology.fulfillment: The worshiper came to the temple with burnt offerings to keep a promise made in distress. The New Testament transfers the language. Believers offer 'a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name,' Hebrews 13:15, and their bodies as a living sacrifice, Romans 12:1. The escalation is that the offerings themselves point to the one sacrifice, Hebrews 10:10-14, which makes the whole system of bulls and goats unnecessary. The type falls short because the animals of verse 15 could not cleanse a conscience, Hebrews 10:4, and so no amount of vowing could settle the debt of sin.

typology.type: The invitation to the nations, verses 1 to 5
typology.fulfillment: The call 'Make a joyful noise to God, all the earth' reaches beyond Israel, and verses 4 and 8 have the peoples bowing and blessing. In the gospel this happens. Paul quotes the psalm family in Romans 15:9-11, and Revelation 15:3-4 has the nations worshiping 'before You.' The escalation is that the call is no longer to come to a place, Jerusalem, but to a person, Matthew 28:19 and Acts 1:8. The type falls short in that the psalm can only invite, while the risen Christ actually sends and gathers.

study.christ:
Psalm 66 does not quote a single word as prophecy of Christ, yet its patterns are the patterns of the gospel. Start with the path through water and fire. Isaiah 43:2 promises the same thing the psalm remembers, and the Lord who says it there is the Redeemer, verse 1. Jesus is the one person who goes all the way through those waters. He speaks of His death as a baptism He must undergo, Luke 12:50, and the psalm's line 'You let men ride over our heads' has its sharpest echo in the mocking and scourging of the passion, Matthew 27:27-31. Yet the psalm does not end in the water. 'You brought us into abundance' finds its fullest form in resurrection, Acts 2:24, and in Christ's promise of life 'to the full,' John 10:10.

Second, Christ is the one through whom the refining is turned into hope. Because He has gone through suffering as a human being, He is able to help those who are being tested, Hebrews 2:18, and to sympathise with weakness, Hebrews 4:15-16. The believer who reads verses 10 to 12 does not read them as a stoic but as a person who has a great high priest who has been through the net and the burden. And the promise of Romans 8:28-39 is the New Testament's commentary on the same movement: trouble, hardship and sword, yet 'more than conquerors through Him who loved us.'

Third, the question of a clean heart in verse 18 leads to Christ, because it is He who makes the approach to God possible for people whose hearts are not clean. The worshiper can say 'God has surely heard' because God's chesed, verse 20, is finally revealed in a person. John 14:13-14 gives the disciples the right to pray in His name, and Hebrews 10:19-22 invites them to draw near with a sincere heart, 'having our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience.' The psalm asks for an honest heart. The gospel supplies the cleansing that makes honesty bearable.

Finally, the missionary sweep of verses 1 to 8 comes true in Christ. The Lord who commanded the nations to be discipled, Matthew 28:18-20, is the one to whom every knee will bow, Philippians 2:10-11. A caution is needed here. The psalm is not a veiled prediction of one event, and it is better to say that Christ carries its themes to their goal than that He is hidden in each line. Where the psalm says 'we' and 'I,' it is the people of God speaking, and Jesus is both the leader who goes first through the water and the one who brings them into the place of abundance.
study.god:
Psalm 66 has a large doctrine of God's rule. He is the Lord of the nations, verse 7, and He is the Lord of the individual heart, verse 18, and the psalm sees no tension between the two. His eyes 'watch the nations,' which means that no rebellious power acts unseen. And the same attentiveness that watches a world watches one prayer: 'He has attended to the sound of my prayer,' verse 19. A God who could only manage empires would be remote, and a God who only listened to individuals would be small. The psalm proclaims both.

The psalm is also honest about a hard edge of His sovereignty. Verses 10 to 12 attribute the net, the burdens and the conquest to God Himself, with a string of 'You' verbs. This is not cruelty, as the last line makes clear, but it does mean the psalm refuses to explain suffering by taking God out of it. It holds together what is often separated: that God is good, that He is in control of the dark season, and that the dark season is not the end. Other Scripture keeps the balance by insisting that God does not delight in affliction, Lamentations 3:31-33, and that He never tempts anyone to sin, James 1:13. The testing in this psalm is not a temptation to evil. It is refining, with a goal in view.

The psalm shows what God is like as a hearer. He listens to the prayer that comes from an honest heart, and He has not 'withheld' His loving devotion. The closing word, chesed, is the anchor. It means covenant faithfulness, the kind of love that binds itself by promise. Because He is like this, a believer can pray in the middle of the fire without pretending that the fire is pleasant.

For worship this has practical shape. The psalm teaches us to start with God's deeds, not our feelings: 'Come and see,' before 'Come and listen.' It teaches that praise is owed in public, that vows made to God should be kept, and that a testimony is a gift to other sufferers. And it shows that the God who rules the nations is approachable enough for the most private cry, which is why the congregation can say 'Blessed be God' and mean it.

crossReferences.note: The sea turned into dry land. Israel went through on dry ground with walls of water on either side. The psalm's 'they passed through the waters on foot' compresses that scene, and 'there we rejoiced in Him' invites every later singer to stand on that shore.

The Jordan was cut off as the priests stepped in, and the people crossed on dry ground. Together with the Red Sea it frames the wilderness years between two crossings, and it lets the psalm's single phrase about passing through the waters recall both ends of the journey.

God promises His presence for the very journey the psalm remembers: through the waters, through the rivers, through the fire. The psalm looks back on deliverance and Isaiah promises it ahead, so the two together show a pattern that holds for every generation of God's people.

'I have refined you, but not as silver.' The prophet uses the same image of the furnace, but he corrects it: God refined His people for His own sake and with a purpose beyond the trial. It pairs with Psalm 66:10 as a reminder that the testing serves a larger aim than punishment.

A remnant is brought through the fire and refined like silver, and then they call on God's name and He answers. The order matches the psalm's movement from testing to answered prayer, and it looks ahead to the day when the covenant is restored in full.

Peter says faith, more precious than gold, is tested by fire, and the result is praise, glory and honour when Christ is revealed. The image has moved from Israel's history to the individual believer, but the logic is unchanged: trials refine, and what remains is praise.

The cup 'overflows,' with the same noun that stands behind 'abundance' in Psalm 66:12. Put side by side, the two show that the end of the dark road is not bare survival but a table, a cup and a fullness that is given by God.

Sin makes a separation, so that God 'will not listen.' It gives the background to Psalm 66:18, and it shows that the psalmist's talk of cherished iniquity draws on a wider prophetic teaching about how sin and prayer are connected.

'Through Jesus, therefore, let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name.' The vow of Psalm 66:13-15 is transposed into a new key: the animals are gone, but the public praise of the lips remains, offered now through Christ.

The song of Moses and of the Lamb ends with the nations coming to worship, because God's righteous acts have been revealed. It is the goal toward which Psalm 66:1-5 points, where the whole earth is called to see His deeds and bow.

Another thanksgiving for deliverance, with a vow paid 'in the presence of all His people' and in the courts of the LORD's house. It helps explain why Psalm 66:13-16 has a vow paid in public, and why the delivered person wants others to hear.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 66 sits at a point in the Bible's story where God's people are between two great movements, rescue and arrival. It answers a question that arises after the exodus and the conquest: what about the years in which God's people seem to be caught in a net, with enemies riding over them? The psalm says that those years too belong to God's purpose, and that they end in a place of abundance. It is a short theology of exile and return, and it is written so that later generations could sing it as their own.

It also answers something older. In Genesis 12:3 God promised that all the families of the earth would be blessed through Abraham, and in Genesis 1 and 2 the whole earth was made as a place where He would be known. Psalm 66 opens with the first breaking through the second: the whole earth is invited to see what God has done for one people. The nations are not an afterthought. They are the audience for whom the deeds were done.

What it sets up is the gospel pattern of passing through death to life. The path through water and fire reaches its sharpest form in Christ, who descends into the flood for His people, Psalm 69:1-2 and Mark 10:38, and comes out on the far side. The psalm's pivot from 'we' to 'I' is also a sign of what salvation does: it gathers a people, and it names each person. In Acts the church prays and is heard, Acts 4:23-31, and in Acts 16:25 Paul and Silas sing in prison, which is almost a live performance of verses 10 to 20.

It ends in new creation. The Bible's last vision has the nations walking by the light of the city, Revelation 21:24, and the song of Moses and the Lamb sung beside a sea of glass, Revelation 15:2-4. The sea that Israel crossed on dry land has become a still sea where the redeemed stand. In the new Jerusalem there is no more curse, no more testing by fire, and a people who can say together, and each one for himself, 'Blessed be God, who has not rejected my prayer or withheld from me His loving devotion.'

quiz.q: What historical event does the psalm recall in verse 6?

options.text: God turning the sea into dry land so His people passed through on foot.
options.note: This recalls the exodus deliverance through the Red Sea, Exodus 14:21-22.

options.text: The building of Solomon's temple.
options.note: The verse describes a sea crossing, not a temple's construction.

options.text: The giving of the law at Sinai.
options.note: The verse specifically recalls passing through the sea, not the giving of the law.

options.text: The conquest of Jericho's walls.
options.note: The verse describes a sea crossing, a different event from the fall of Jericho.

quiz.q: How does the psalm describe God's testing of His people, in verse 10?

options.text: You have refined us like silver.
options.note: This pictures deliberate, purposeful testing that removes impurity, like the refining of precious metal.

options.text: You have abandoned us to random chance.
options.note: The image is purposeful refining, not abandonment to chance.

options.text: You have hidden us from every trial.
options.note: The psalm describes real testing endured, not the avoidance of all trial.

options.text: You have punished us without any purpose.
options.note: The refining image specifically implies purpose, removing impurity, not purposeless punishment.

quiz.q: What does verse 12 say is the outcome of going 'through fire and water'?

options.text: God brought them into abundance.
options.note: The trial ends not in destruction but in overflowing provision.

options.text: They were left permanently in hardship.
options.note: The verse explicitly names abundance as the outcome, not ongoing hardship.

options.text: They lost everything they once had.
options.note: The verse describes gain, abundance, as the trial's outcome, not loss.

options.text: They were scattered among the nations.
options.note: The specific outcome named is abundance, not scattering.

quiz.q: What condition does the psalmist name for God hearing his prayer, in verse 18?

options.text: Not cherishing iniquity in his heart.
options.note: The psalmist ties answered prayer to an honestly kept heart, not sinless perfection.

options.text: Offering the largest possible sacrifice.
options.note: While sacrifices are mentioned earlier, verse 18 specifically names the heart's honesty as the condition.

options.text: Being born into a priestly family.
options.note: No such requirement is mentioned; the condition named is the heart's honesty.

options.text: Praying only in the temple in Jerusalem.
options.note: The condition given is the heart's integrity, not the specific location of prayer.

quiz.q: How does this psalm's picture of deliverance through the sea and through fire and water connect to Christ?

options.text: Christ accomplishes the greater exodus, leading His people through death itself into resurrection life.
options.note: This fulfills the pattern of deliverance through trial into abundance that both the exodus and the psalmist's testimony display.

options.text: Christ has no connection to deliverance through trial in the New Testament.
options.note: Romans 8:37 and Luke 9:31 both connect Christ directly to deliverance through trial into greater life.

options.text: Christ promises His followers will never face any fire or water, any trial at all.
options.note: The New Testament promises deliverance through trials, not the absence of all trials, 1 Peter 1:6-7.

options.text: Christ's death is entirely unrelated to the theme of testing or refining.
options.note: 1 Peter 1:6-7 explicitly connects the refining of faith through trials to the pattern fulfilled in Christ.

questions: The psalm calls 'all the earth' to make a joyful noise and come see what God has done, verses 1 and 5. What specific thing has God done in your life recently that is worth telling someone else about this week?

God refines His people like silver, verse 10, a purposeful process rather than random suffering. How does viewing your current difficulty as purposeful refining, rather than meaningless hardship, change how you endure it?

The psalm testifies that trials end not in destruction but in abundance, 'You brought us into abundance,' verse 12. Where do you need to trust that your current fire and water will lead somewhere good, even if you cannot see it yet?

The psalmist ties answered prayer to not cherishing sin in his heart, verse 18. Is there anything you are currently holding onto, rather than confessing honestly to God, that may be affecting your own prayer life?

The psalm moves from corporate praise, 'all the earth,' to deeply personal testimony, 'I will declare what He has done for me,' verse 16. What is your own personal testimony of what God has done that you could share with someone this week?

translationNotes.note: Refined renders tsaraph, the smelting process that removes impurity from precious metal through intense heat, a deliberate image of purposeful, productive testing.
Praised Him with my tongue can also be rendered and His praise was on my tongue, either reading emphasizing that praise accompanied the cry for help rather than following only after deliverance.
Iniquity renders aven, often tied elsewhere to idolatry or deceit; cherished implies deliberate holding onto sin rather than the ordinary imperfection every believer carries and confesses.
